reference: 2025 curriculum: vocabulary appendix pp.73–129; grammar appendix pp.133–137. Product rubric and examples below are authored for WordBot, not official exam items or psychometrically calibrated difficulty labels.
audience: A learner who has completed Chinese senior-high compulsory and selective-compulsory English. The target word/sense may be new; understanding the setting, decisive clues and distractors must not require additional unsupported specialist knowledge.
rules: Evaluate vocabulary IN ITS ACTUAL SENSE and collocation, syntax, inference/background knowledge, and ALL distractors. Assuming the learner knows the target sense, can they understand the clues and distinguish the choices?

Use the local vocabulary hints as evidence, not a whitelist. Listed words can have unfamiliar senses. Unlisted names, transparent derivations, explained terms and incidental details can be acceptable. Do not impose a one-new-word rule or a count/percentage threshold.

Do not reject by sentence length, number of clauses, punctuation or historical/religious/scientific topic. Prefer natural meaningful context. Identify an actual comprehension barrier, not merely a long or rare-looking word.

Core clues should remain accessible without knowing another harder unglossed word. A cluster of unfamiliar terms can obstruct understanding even when no single term is indispensable. Do not exempt distractors just because the target is advanced.

Use suitable only when all four dimensions are supported. Borderline means a concrete unresolved comprehension concern; unsuitable means an identified blocking requirement. Replace only the problematic context or distractors; preserve the target meaning. Do not make the item ambiguous to simplify it.
grammarReference: Compulsory/selective-compulsory scope includes ordinary tenses and passive voice, infinitives, -ing/-ed forms, coordination, object/adverbial/relative/subject/predicative clauses and ellipsis. Appositive clauses, inversion, emphasis and subjunctive are marked elective-improvement (***) in this appendix: inspect their actual comprehension demands rather than automatically rejecting their presence. There is no sentence-word-count ceiling.

examples.context: Although the old books were damaged, the scribe copied every page by hand so that future readers could still read the stories.
examples.assessment: Suitable language support: clear familiar action and clause relationships despite length. This is a stem example only; answer uniqueness depends on the options.

examples.context: At the monastery, the scribe copied an old book by hand.
examples.assessment: The unfamiliar location can be incidental: copied/book/by hand remain understandable. Do not reject merely for monastery or historical subject matter.

examples.context: The scribe transcribed illuminated manuscripts onto vellum.
examples.assessment: Unsuitable support if the learner must decode transcribed/manuscripts/vellum to understand the action; use accessible action/material descriptions. No permanent banned-word list.

examples.context: The clerk recorded the deposition before the court granted a stay.
examples.assessment: Inspect deposition and the legal sense of stay, even if stay is listed. If this unexplained legal process blocks comprehension, revise the context.
